newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SE Asian trade awaits USDA report, El Nino a worry.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian trade awaits USDA report, El Nino a worry.

text.p: The Southeast Asian grains and oilseeds business was quiet on Thursday as buyers sat back to wait for the monthly U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) crop report due out later in the day, traders said.
"People are not going to come in until they see the USDA report. A lot of people are expecting production to be good and carryout to be higher," one trader said.
Indonesia was said to have bought last week a combined shipment of soymeal, at around $310 a tonne C&F, and corn for July shipment, another trader said.
But other dealers could not confirm the report.
"I'm not saying it was not done. But that seems unlikely since they have enough corn and they're just waiting for their harvest," one said.

Dealers said Indonesia would need to buy, from August onwards, about 50,000 to 90,000 tonnes of meal. Thailand would still need a few cargoes of meal while Malaysia may be in for 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes.
"August is not so well covered for Indonesia and Malaysia is only half-covered for that month," a dealer said.
Thailand, on the other hand, has covered about 50-60 percent of its soymeal needs for August, dealers said.

Regional buyers will probably wait for the USDA report to come out to confirm what they feel is a strong bearish trend in the soymeal and soybeans market. The trade is also focused on China, which has bought an estimated 300,000 tonnes of soymeal.
"They're waiting for prices to come down. The bearish sentiment in the market is pretty strong," another dealer said.
"People here are going to buy South American, not the U.S.," a trader added.

The corn market is moribund in the region with Malaysia overflowing with supplies, Thailand well-covered and Indonesia waiting for its harvest from East Java and in no hurry to lock up imports for the second half of 1997.
"Corn is dead in the region," a dealer said.
Some people in the trade expressed concern about the possible impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon on crops in Indonesia and the Philippines, the two biggest buyers of wheat in Southeast Asia.
"There was a bad drought in Indonesia and the Philippines in 1983," one dealer said. "This will pose a big problem for Indonesia's rice harvests. In fact, all their crops will be affected."

The El Nino, which usually results when a warm ocean current appears off the South American coast, disrupts normal weather patterns around the world and can wreak havoc on farms around the Asia-Pacific region.
Named after the Christ child by Peruvian anchovy fishermen because of its appearance around Christmas time, the last major El Nino began in late 1991.

The most devastating in recent memory was the one in 1983, blighting Indonesia, South Africa, Australia and the Philippines with a blistering drought and triggering floods in South America and India which caused billions of dollars of damage.

"They were able to irrigate some areas in Indonesia, but a large part of their farms still depend on rainwater. The same is true of the Philippines," one dealer said. "They are vulnerable to a dry spell."
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
